newsitem.title: BELGIUM: African franc zone says no fear of Euro.
newsitem.headline: African franc zone says no fear of Euro.

text.p: Europe's adoption of a single currency will not jeopardise the 50-year-old African franc that is tied to its French counterpart, a leading African central banker said on Thursday.

"The creation of the Euro does not put into question the relations with France," the governor of the central bank of the West African States, Charles Konan Banny, said in an interveiw with a small group of reporters.

Top European Union and French officials have firmly pledged that when the Euro, the EU's single currency, is introduced in 1999 the CFA franc will simply be pegged to the Euro instead of the old French currency.
EU monetary affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy told the conference: "The arrival of the euro will not in any way change currency relations in the African states."
He added, however, that should there be a change in the system, the future European Central Bank would need to be consulted.
Konan Banny was less certain about what would happen to the value of the CFA franc, which links 14 former French colonies in the sub-saharan Africa.
Asked whether the African franc should devalue ahead of the EU's monetary union to avoid it being pushed up with a strong Euro, Konan Banny simply said: "I don't have any idea".

"Giscard d'Estaing is the one who has an opinion about devaluation matters," he added referring to former French president Valery Giscard-d'Estaing's remarks in a magazine interview made public on Wednesday that the French franc should be devalued before being merged in the Euro.
Konan Banny said the CFA franc was stable after the trauma of the devaluation in January 1994, the first against the French franc since World War Two.
"It is stable and this is demonstrated by the economic situation," he said.
But he would not be drawn on whether floating the currency was an option. "You can have different monetary regimes. The choice is political".

Although the CFA franc is used in 14 African countries, Konan Banny is more directly in charge of the monetary policy of half of those countries which in 1994 created the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU). The central bank of the west African CFA franc countries is in Dakar, in Senegal.
WAEMU groups Benin, Burkina Faso, the Ivory Coast, Mali, Niger, Senegal and Togo. Other African countries that use the CFA franc include Gabon, Cameroun and Congo.
Konan Banny urged the national governments of WAEMU to promote a greater convergence of their economies as the group moves to integrate further.

He expected economic growth in the zone would be 5.7 percent this year, slightly higher on 5.6 percent in 1995, and that average inflation would be down to five percent in 1996 and three percent in 1997.
